transcript:
Header: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~75m | Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (CTO, Aurelius), Anna Liu (Platform), Maya Patel (Security), Devon Park (Infra)

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, looks like we have most folks. quick agenda — private vpc networking, control plane vs data plane, nat/egress, dns, and then runtime perf details: kv cache, batching, quantization tradeoffs. feel free to interrupt, we'll go deep.

00:22 Carlos: yeah thanks, Jordan. quick context — we're looking to run Redwood Private in our AWS VPC, want guarantees on latency and no outbound data to public networks, also need integration with our KMS. tradeoffs on whether to go with interface endpoints or transit gateway.

00:45 Priya: got it. high-level — Redwood Private uses a control-plane channel (we call it the control plane) that can be either via PrivateLink/Interface endpoint or via our customer-managed connector if you want zero cross-account egress. the inference data path is entirely inside customer VPC for dedicated nodes; control plane telemetry can be routed through PrivateLink. is that the constraint?

01:10 Anna: yes, we need control-plane meta only over PrivateLink, and model artifacts must be pulled from our S3 via VPC endpoint or via an internal repo. also subnet sizing — we use /20s in many clusters but worried about ENI/IP exhaustion when we spin many GPU nodes.

01:33 Priya: right — two common patterns: 1) use interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Redwood control plane APIs and ECR/S3 access via gateway endpoints; 2) use a Transit Gateway when you have multi-account and want centralized routing. for IPs: our recommendation is keep separate private subnets for Redwood worker pools, plan for ~4-6 ENIs per GPU node depending on instance type — that drives your ip plan. in practice we see teams pick a /22 per pool to start and expand.

02:05 Devon: can you explain the 4-6 ENIs thing? that's a surprise, we thought each instance had 1 primary only.

02:18 Priya: yeah, it's because our runtime attaches multiple network interfaces for high throughput and zero-copy NVLink proxied metrics and sometimes an ENI is reserved for control plane, one for model fetch traffic, and the primary. this also comes from CNI plugin behavior, and if you're using GKE or EKS with trunking, the numbers vary. sorry if that was fuzzy earlier — it's not always 6, it's a function of instance and CNI.

02:45 Liam: adding — for egress to public model stores or third-party telemetry endpoints, we recommend NAT Gateway in a controlled egress subnet, or better, VPC endpoints so traffic never leaves Amazon's backbone. NAT adds cost and hops which affect tail latency slightly.

03:05 Maya: from security perspective we need mTLS for control plane, no direct internet egress from worker subnets, and audit logs to our SIEM. can Redwood integrate with our KMS for model keys? and do you support HSM-backed keys?

03:22 Jordan: yes — KMS integration is supported; we can do envelope encryption with customer KMS, and for HSM we have patterns to integrate with AWS CloudHSM or external HSM via a gateway. audit logs — we can ship detailed audit events to a customer S3 or to your logging collector via a private endpoint. we'll share the exact schema.

03:45 Carlos: switching to runtime perf — our main goal is 99th percentile latency under 150ms for single-turn chat with ~512 token context for smallish model family. what are realistic expectations with a private deployment?

04:03 Priya: a few levers: batching config, KV cache hit rate, quantization profile, and instance type/GPU memory. for low latency you want small max batch sizes and pre-warmed KV caches. our continuous-batching mode collects micro-batches every 10-20ms — that can reduce cost but increase p99. if you need strict p99, set prefer_latency true and reduce batch size and batch timeouts.

04:34 Liam: also kernel selection and sequence length matter. if most requests are short (<=128) you get much better throughput. for 512 tokens, plan more memory and consider int8 quantization; int4 can save memory but may slightly increase latency from dequantization overhead in certain kernels. transcription note: some of this was 'de-qua nization' in the auto notes.

05:00 Anna: about KV cache — how warm is it after a restart, what's the warm-up time, and how do you recommend priming caches for critical endpoints? we have many short lived model versions.

05:15 Priya: KV cache is per-model-version per-host; on restart it's cold. warm-up comes from observed traffic or proactive priming. we provide a prime API and a 'cache population' utility. priming with typical prefixes yields >90% hit-rates for steady workloads. if you have many versions, consider a canary pool with preloaded cache and auto-failover. note there's a small memory overhead per cached KV shard.

05:44 Carlos: for canary pools — do you recommend separate subnets or same subnet? isolate by security groups?

05:55 Priya: isolate logically with security groups and IAM roles; subnet separation only if you need different route tables or NACLs. often teams keep same VPC private subnet but separate ASG/node group.

06:10 Devon: we use private DNS resolvers internally and have split-horizon for certain domains — any gotchas for PrivateLink and DNS?

06:22 Priya: yes — PrivateLink uses interface endpoints with private DNS option. if you enable private DNS, it creates ENIs with a private hostname that maps to the endpoint. split-horizon can shadow that, so we recommend explicit VPC resolver rules or use a dedicated resolver for Redwood control plane endpoints. also watch your DNS TTLs during rolling updates.

06:45 Maya: what about health checks and load balancer ports? our security team likes to know what ports to open.

06:53 Liam: our worker agents communicate on a few ports (we'll include in the doc). typically health probes are HTTP on 8080/9090, control API on 443 via PrivateLink, and internal runtime metrics on a port the customer controls and can restrict to monitoring subnets. we recommend SG rules allowing controller IPs only or interface endpoint security groups.

07:15 Carlos: quantify latency impact of PrivateLink vs public TLS: is there measurable overhead?

07:23 Priya: PrivateLink is usually faster — keeps traffic on the AZ/region private net — but interface endpoints introduce an extra ENI hop; latency delta is often <1-3ms compared to public TLS through the internet, but it depends on path (if you route via NAT+internet vs PrivateLink). so PrivateLink is preferred for p99-sensitive workloads.

07:45 Anna: ok, switching to batching — how do we choose batch size vs model concurrency? we saw some spikes where latency jumped during peak.

07:55 Priya: rule of thumb: pick max_batch_size so that expected latency under normal load stays under your SLO; set max_batch_wait_ms low (5-20ms) for latency-sensitive routes. use adaptive batching for throughput-oriented routes. you can also set per-route configs in the config map and Redwood runtime will honor route-priority for backpressure. backlog-based autoscaling helps if you're getting queueing.

08:25 Devon: does batch packing across requests from different customers (multi-tenant) happen? we need strict tenant isolation.

08:34 Jordan: in Private deployments for enterprise you can opt for single-tenant worker pools per customer; otherwise we do tenant-aware batching but never mix sensitive extractions across tenant boundaries unless configured. we'll document isolation guarantees.

08:50 Maya: quantization — what accuracy regression do you see with int8 vs int4, and do you support mixed precision?

09:00 Priya: int8 is mature for most open models — sub 1% perplexity delta in many cases, int4 can vary more and we recommend evals. we support mixed precision and per-layer tuning — Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles by workload. quantized models can reduce memory and improve throughput but watch for sampling variance in generation tasks. we'll share a sample quant report.

09:25 Carlos: networking again — model artifacts fetch path. we want no public S3 access. can the runtime fetch from a private S3 endpoint and use VPC endpoint policies?

09:36 Liam: yes — we support pulling from S3 via gateway endpoint or from an internal artifact repo (your registries). you can lock access with endpoint policies and IAM roles. if you're using ECR, use interface endpoint for ECR and S3 gateway for objects.

09:58 Anna: any specific recommendations for subnet sizes for, say, 50 GPU nodes?

10:05 Priya: rough math — if each node ends up using ~3 ENIs on average and you plan for 20% headroom, for 50 nodes that's 50 * 3 * 1.2 = 180 IPs. /24 = 256 addresses is sufficient but consider separating pools by AZ (eg three /26s per AZ could be tight). I'd recommend at least /24 per worker pool to avoid surprises. we'll include a sizing calc in the follow-up.

10:30 Carlos: what about cross-AZ traffic — does Redis/KV cache replication add latency?

10:40 Priya: KV cache is local to the host for fastest token lookup; for shared cache you can co-locate caches in the same AZ or use a regional cache with replication TTLs. cross-AZ reads add ~1-4ms typical; for p99 you'd prefer AZ-local cache and sticky routing to same AZ when possible.

11:05 Maya: audit and compliance — can we get signed audit logs and support for retention policies? also, does Redwood keep any PII?

11:15 Jordan: we can configure retention and signed logs. Redwood Private by default does not send customer input to Redwood's hosted logs unless you opt in; logs can be pushed to your bucket and we can redact PII or leave raw per agreement. we'll send our security whitepaper and SOC2 attestation.

11:40 Anna: last technical — if we run benchmarks, what metrics should we collect and what baseline do you suggest?

11:50 Liam: collect p50/p95/p99, tail latency, CPU/GPU utilization, GPU memory, KV cache hit-rate, batch sizes over time, network egress and latencies, and errors per route. baseline: run a 24h steady-state with synthetic traffic that mirrors arrival distribution and a ramp test for spikes. we'll provide the benchmark harness.

12:15 Jordan: ok let's do a quick recap and next steps. action items: Priya will send a subnet/IP sizing doc and recommended templates; Jordan will send benchmark spreadsheet and security docs; Anna to share VPC/CIDR info; Maya to consolidate compliance Qs; we'll schedule the benchmark kickoff next week.

12:40 Carlos: sounds good, thanks everyone. this was helpful.

12:50 Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors e.g., 'KV catch' instead of KV cache, 'de-qua nization' instead of dequantization, 'Private Link' variant spellings. Links shared in chat: deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/aurelius-private-vpc.pdf , security pack: https://redwood.example.com/sec/soc2.pdf , benchmark sheet: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/aurelius-template.xlsx

13:05 End of call.
